en.title: Master of Business Administration (MBA): the whole course
en.short: What an MBA covers, how it is organised and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
The Master of Business Administration, or MBA, is a master’s-level general management degree. It prepares people to make decisions across the whole business, not only in one function. A finance manager must understand marketing; a marketing manager must understand costs and cash flow. The MBA teaches that wider view.

Students usually enter with a first degree, sometimes in another field. The course therefore starts each topic from its foundations and then moves to master’s depth. It is a professional degree. Teaching often uses cases, group projects, simulations and presentations, though some programmes include research methods and a dissertation or consulting project.

The aim is judgement. An MBA should help you ask the right question, use evidence, weigh trade-offs and explain a decision clearly.

sections.heading: How the programme is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and award titles differ by country and institution. Programmes are offered full-time, part-time, executive and online. In Nigeria, many university MBAs run for about two years full-time, with part-time and executive formats taking longer. In the United States, a full-time MBA is often two years; in the United Kingdom, many full-time MBAs are one year. These are common patterns, not rules.

Admission requirements also vary. Some schools require work experience; others admit strong graduates directly. In Nigeria, the National Universities Commission regulates university programmes. Some business schools also hold accreditation from bodies such as AACSB, AMBA or EQUIS. Check your own handbook for duration, credit units, fees, attendance rules and whether a project or internship is required.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
A common order starts with the language of business. Managerial economics gives the tools of demand, cost and market structure. Financial reporting and analysis shows how to read statements. Managerial accounting and control covers budgets, costs and performance. Corporate finance and valuation deals with investment, financing and value.

The next block looks outward and inward. Marketing management and customer value, operations and process management, and supply chain management show how goods and services reach customers. Organisational behaviour and managing people, strategic human resource management, and leadership and organisational change cover the human side.

Governance and law follow: business ethics and corporate governance, and business law and compliance for managers. Data and digital topics come next: business analytics and data-driven decisions, and information systems and digital transformation.

The final block integrates. Strategic management and corporate strategy, growth and acquisitions set direction. International business and global strategy adds the cross-border view. Entrepreneurship and innovation management, project management, negotiation and conflict resolution, enterprise risk management, and sustainability and environmental, social and governance (ESG) in business build specialist judgement. Managerial communication and persuasion, research methods for business, and business policy and integrative decision-making bring the course together.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study each topic twice. First learn the foundation: the definition, the framework and one worked example. Then apply it to a real or realistic case. For quantitative topics, redo calculations without looking at the answer and check the units. For qualitative topics, write a short argument: issue, evidence, options, recommendation and risk.

Use one company as a running case through the course. A firm you know well, such as a local retailer or a family business, makes abstract ideas concrete. Keep a glossary of terms and a file of examples. Work in groups, but write your own notes. Read cases actively: identify the decision, the constraints and the missing information.

Check current sources for law, tax, regulation and market data. Your exam may test a particular edition or country. Past questions show the expected depth.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make
sections.text:
The most common mistake is memorising frameworks without applying them. An examiner wants a recommendation that follows from the evidence, not a list of models.

Other frequent errors include:
Treating one country’s law or tax rule as universal.
Using old data or an old edition of a textbook.
Confusing correlation with causation in analytics.
Giving a ratio or a calculation without saying what it means.
Ignoring implementation, ethics and stakeholder effects.
Writing long answers with no clear decision.
Letting group work replace your own understanding.

An MBA rewards clear thinking and honest evidence. It does not reward jargon.

keyPoints: An MBA is a general management degree that integrates finance, marketing, operations, people, law and strategy.
Programme length, admission rules and awards differ by country and school, so check your own handbook.
Start each topic from its foundations, then apply it to a case and a clear recommendation.
Quantitative work needs checked calculations; qualitative work needs evidence and trade-offs.
Name the country when a law, tax rule or regulation applies there.
Use current sources and avoid treating a framework as an answer by itself.

en.title: Managerial Economics for Business Decisions
en.short: Demand, elasticity, costs, market structure, pricing power and decisions under risk.

sections.heading: Demand and elasticity
sections.text: Demand is the quantity buyers will take at each price; supply is the quantity sellers will offer. Equilibrium is where the curves cross. Elasticity measures responsiveness. Price elasticity of demand = percentage change in quantity ÷ percentage change in price. If it is greater than 1 in absolute value, demand is elastic, so a price rise cuts revenue. Income elasticity and cross-price elasticity help managers forecast how demand shifts with income or rival prices.

sections.heading: Production and cost
sections.text: In the short run at least one input is fixed. Total cost = fixed cost + variable cost. Average cost = total cost ÷ output; marginal cost is the extra cost of one more unit. Diminishing returns make marginal cost rise. In the long run all inputs can change. Economies of scale lower long-run average cost as output grows; diseconomies raise it. Managers choose the least-cost mix of inputs.

sections.heading: Market power and pricing
sections.text: Market structure ranges from perfect competition to monopoly, with monopolistic competition and oligopoly between. A firm with market power faces a downward-sloping demand curve, so price exceeds marginal revenue. It maximises profit where marginal revenue = marginal cost, then reads price from demand. Markup pricing and price discrimination can raise profit; price discrimination works when buyers differ in willingness to pay and resale is limited.

sections.heading: Risk and worked example
sections.text: Risk means outcomes have known probabilities; uncertainty means they do not. Expected value = Σ probability × payoff. Managers also use sensitivity analysis and risk-adjusted discount rates. Worked example: demand P = 100 − 2Q, so MR = 100 − 4Q. Total cost TC = 20Q, so MC = 20. Set MR = MC: 100 − 4Q = 20, Q = 20. Price P = 100 − 40 = 60. Profit = (60 − 20) × 20 = 800. At this point elasticity is −1.5, so demand is elastic.

keyPoints: Price elasticity = percentage change in quantity ÷ percentage change in price.
Profit is maximised where marginal revenue = marginal cost.
Short-run costs separate fixed and variable cost; long-run costs show economies of scale.
Market structure shapes pricing power; a downward-sloping demand curve makes price exceed marginal revenue.
Expected value = Σ probability × payoff.
Use sensitivity analysis when probabilities are uncertain.

en.title: Financial Reporting and Analysis for Managers
en.short: Reading annual reports, accrual accounting, key ratios and accounting quality.

sections.heading: Reading the report
sections.text: An annual report contains the financial statements, notes, directors’ report and auditor’s report. The statement of financial position lists assets, liabilities and equity at a date. The statement of profit or loss shows income and expenses over a period. The statement of cash flows shows cash receipts and payments. The notes explain accounting policies and estimates. IFRS is used in many countries, but local rules differ, so check the jurisdiction.

sections.heading: Accrual accounting
sections.text: Accrual accounting records revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, not when cash moves. Revenue recognition usually requires a transfer of goods or services to a customer and a reliably measurable amount. Expenses are matched to the revenue they help produce. Estimates for depreciation, bad debts and warranties affect profit. The cash flow statement reconciles profit to cash and reveals timing differences. A sale on credit raises profit before cash arrives.

sections.heading: Worked example: ratios
sections.text:
Example figures for Adeyemi Ltd, in naira:
Revenue 1,000,000
Gross profit 300,000
Operating profit 120,000
Finance cost 20,000
Current assets 250,000
Inventory 100,000
Current liabilities 150,000
Equity 400,000
Long-term debt 200,000
Cash from operations 90,000

Gross margin = 300,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 30%.
Operating margin = 120,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 12%.
Return on capital employed = 120,000 ÷ (400,000 + 200,000) = 20%.
Current ratio = 250,000 ÷ 150,000 = 1.67.
Quick ratio = (250,000 − 100,000) ÷ 150,000 = 1.00.
Gearing = 200,000 ÷ 600,000 = 33.3%.
Interest cover = 120,000 ÷ 20,000 = 6 times.
Cash conversion = 90,000 ÷ 120,000 = 0.75.

sections.heading: Quality and limits
sections.text: Compare profit with operating cash flow. If receivables or inventory grow faster than revenue, check collection and obsolescence. Look for changes in accounting policy, one-off gains, aggressive revenue recognition and off-balance-sheet finance. Read the auditor’s opinion. Ratios need comparators, industry context and awareness that historical cost and inflation can distort them.

keyPoints: Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue; operating margin = operating profit ÷ revenue.
ROCE = operating profit ÷ capital employed, where capital employed is equity plus long-term debt.
Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities; quick ratio excludes inventory.
Gearing = long-term debt ÷ (debt + equity); interest cover = operating profit ÷ finance cost.
Cash conversion = cash from operations ÷ operating profit; falling conversion warns of earnings quality risk.
Always read the notes and auditor’s report and compare ratios with prior years and peers.

en.title: Managerial Accounting and Control
en.short: Cost behaviour, break-even, relevant costing, budgets, variances and responsibility centres for managers.

sections.heading: Cost behaviour and contribution
sections.text: Cost behaviour describes how a cost changes with activity. Variable costs change in total with output, fixed costs stay constant within a relevant range, and mixed costs have both parts. Contribution margin is sales revenue minus variable costs. Contribution per unit is selling price minus variable cost per unit. It shows what each sale adds towards fixed costs and profit. Managers use it for short-term decisions, because fixed costs do not change in that range.

sections.heading: Break-even and relevant costing
sections.text: Break-even is the sales volume where total contribution equals fixed costs and profit is zero. Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit. Relevant costing includes only future cash flows that differ between alternatives. Sunk costs and allocated fixed costs are excluded. Example: price ₦500, variable cost ₦300, fixed costs ₦200,000. Contribution per unit = ₦200. Break-even = 200,000 ÷ 200 = 1,000 units. At 1,200 units, profit = (1,200 × 200) − 200,000 = ₦40,000.

sections.heading: Budgeting and variances
sections.text: Budgeting is a plan in quantities and money for a future period. Variance analysis compares actual results with the budget. A price variance measures the effect of paying or charging a different price. A volume variance measures the effect of selling a different quantity. Example: budgeted sales 1,200 units at ₦500; actual 1,100 units at ₦520. Revenue variance = 572,000 − 600,000 = ₦28,000 adverse. Price variance = (520 − 500) × 1,100 = ₦22,000 favourable. Volume variance = (1,100 − 1,200) × 500 = ₦50,000 adverse. Check: 22,000 − 50,000 = −28,000.

sections.heading: Responsibility centres
sections.text: Responsibility centres assign accountability. A cost centre controls costs, a revenue centre controls revenue, a profit centre controls both, and an investment centre also controls invested capital. Managers should be judged on items they control, called the controllability principle. Budgets set targets, variances signal problems, and responsibility centres connect results to the manager accountable for them. Performance measures must avoid encouraging harmful short-term actions.

keyPoints: Contribution per unit = selling price − variable cost per unit; contribution margin = sales − variable costs.
Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit, and profit = (units × contribution per unit) − fixed costs.
Relevant costing uses only future cash flows that differ between alternatives; ignore sunk costs and allocated fixed costs.
A price variance = (actual price − standard price) × actual quantity; a volume variance = (actual quantity − budgeted quantity) × standard price.
Responsibility centres are cost, revenue, profit and investment centres, and managers should be judged on controllable items.
Budgets set targets and variances explain differences between actual and planned performance.

en.title: Corporate Finance and Valuation
en.short: Time value, NPV, WACC, capital structure, dividends and firm valuation models.

sections.heading: Time value
sections.text:
Money today can be invested, so it is worth more than the same money later. Future value = present value × (1 + r)^n. Present value = future cash flow ÷ (1 + r)^n, where r is the discount rate and n the number of periods.

Discount each cash flow and add them up to value a stream.

sections.heading: Capital budgeting
sections.text:
Capital budgeting chooses long-term projects. Net present value (NPV) is discounted cash flows minus initial outlay. Accept positive NPV projects. Internal rate of return (IRR) makes NPV zero. Payback ignores later cash flows and time value.

Example: a project costs 1,000,000 and pays 600,000 at the end of years 1 and 2. At 12%, PV = 600,000 ÷ 1.12 + 600,000 ÷ 1.12² = 535,714 + 478,316 = 1,014,030. NPV = 14,030. Accept it.

sections.heading: Cost of capital
sections.text:
WACC is the average return investors require. WACC = (E ÷ V) × Re + (D ÷ V) × Rd × (1 − T). E and D are market values of equity and debt, V = E + D, Re is cost of equity, Rd is cost of debt, T is tax rate.

Example: E = 600m, D = 400m, Re = 15%, Rd = 10%, T = 25%. WACC = 0.6 × 15% + 0.4 × 10% × 0.75 = 9% + 3% = 12%. Cost of equity may use CAPM: Re = Rf + β × (Rm − Rf), where Rf is the risk-free rate, β measures sensitivity to market moves, and Rm − Rf is the market risk premium. WACC assumes stable mix.

sections.heading: Financing and valuation
sections.text:
Capital structure is the debt-equity mix. Modigliani and Miller show that, without taxes, distress costs or market imperfections, the mix does not affect firm value. With taxes, interest relief adds value but distress costs limit debt. Dividend policy sets payout; under the same assumptions it does not affect value, but taxes and signalling matter.

Discounted cash flow values expected free cash flows at WACC to get enterprise value; subtract net debt (debt minus cash) for equity value. Multiples and dividend discount models are alternatives.

keyPoints: Present value = future cash flow ÷ (1 + r)^n, and NPV = present value of cash flows − initial outlay.
Accept a project when its NPV is positive; IRR is the rate that makes NPV zero.
WACC = (E ÷ V) × Re + (D ÷ V) × Rd × (1 − T), using market values and after-tax debt.
Enterprise value = present value of free cash flows at WACC; equity value = enterprise value − net debt.
Under Modigliani and Miller assumptions, capital structure and dividend policy do not affect firm value; taxes, distress costs and signalling can change this.
Valuation models depend on forecasts and assumptions, so check sensitivity.

en.title: Marketing Management and Customer Value
en.short: Segmentation, targeting, positioning, the marketing mix, customer lifetime value, branding and channels.

sections.heading: Segmentation, targeting, positioning
sections.text: Segmentation divides a market into groups with similar needs, using demographic, geographic, psychographic (lifestyle and values) or behavioural bases. Useful segments are measurable, accessible, differentiable, actionable and large enough to serve. Targeting evaluates each segment’s size, growth, profitability, competition and fit with the firm’s resources, then selects one or more. Positioning designs the offer and image to occupy a distinct place in the target customer’s mind. A clear value proposition states the benefits and price relative to alternatives, and positioning must be credible and hard to copy.

sections.heading: Marketing mix and value
sections.text: The marketing mix is the set of controllable tools: product, price, place and promotion. Service offers add people, process and physical evidence. Customer perceived value is total benefits minus total costs. Customer lifetime value (CLV) is the present value of future contribution from a customer. With constant annual margin m, retention rate r and discount rate d, one common simplified formula is CLV = m × r ÷ (1 + d − r). The formula assumes constant margin and retention. Example: m = ₦15,000, r = 0.80, d = 0.10. CLV = 15,000 × 0.80 ÷ (1 + 0.10 − 0.80) = 12,000 ÷ 0.30 = ₦40,000. Check: 0.30 × 40,000 = 12,000. CLV guides how much to spend on acquisition and retention.

sections.heading: Branding, channels, communication
sections.text: A brand is a name, sign or symbol that identifies and differentiates an offer. Brand equity is the added value customers attach to it. Distribution channels move the offer to customers; managers choose coverage, intermediaries and online or physical routes. Channel conflict arises when routes compete for the same customers. Integrated marketing communication (IMC) coordinates advertising, sales promotion, public relations, personal selling and digital messages so they reinforce one another. IMC starts from the customer’s view, not from separate department budgets. An offer is evaluated by segment fit, contribution margin, CLV, channel economics and message consistency.

keyPoints: Segmentation groups customers by similar needs; targeting selects segments; positioning shapes the place in the customer’s mind.
The marketing mix is product, price, place and promotion, extended for services by people, process and physical evidence.
Customer perceived value is benefits minus costs.
CLV = annual margin × retention rate ÷ (1 + discount rate − retention rate), assuming constant values.
A brand identifies and differentiates; brand equity is the added value it creates.
IMC coordinates all messages, and channel choices must match the target segment and margin.

en.title: Operations and Process Management
en.short: Process design, capacity, queues, quality, lean and service operations for improving performance.

sections.heading: Process view
sections.text: An operation turns inputs into outputs. Process design sets the sequence of activities, who does them and where. A process map shows steps, delays and decisions. Little’s Law links work in process (WIP), throughput and flow time: WIP = throughput × flow time. If a clinic treats 40 patients a day and each spends 0.5 day in the system, average WIP = 40 × 0.5 = 20 patients. Capacity is the maximum output in a period. The bottleneck is the lowest-capacity step and it limits the whole process.

sections.heading: Capacity and queues
sections.text: Utilisation = arrival rate ÷ capacity. At 80% utilisation there is spare capacity; at 95% queues and waiting times rise sharply. Queuing theory studies waiting. Even when average demand is below capacity, variability causes queues. Managers reduce waiting by adding capacity, pooling queues, standardising work or scheduling appointments. A bank teller serving 18 customers an hour with capacity 20 an hour has utilisation 18 ÷ 20 = 90%. It is near the steep waiting curve, so small demand rises cause long waits.

sections.heading: Quality and lean
sections.text: Quality means conformance to requirements and fitness for use. It is built into the process, not inspected in at the end. Statistical process control plots measurements over time and signals unusual variation. Lean operations remove waste, such as waiting, overproduction, defects and unnecessary movement. Lean uses pull, where later steps signal demand, and flow, where work moves steadily. It began in manufacturing, notably at Toyota, and is adapted to services.

sections.heading: Service operations
sections.text: Services are intangible, produced and consumed at the same time, variable and perishable. Service design therefore manages customer contact, queues and employee discretion. A Lagos repair shop has three technicians. Each repair takes 2 hours on average. Capacity = 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 repairs per hour. If demand is 1.2 repairs per hour, utilisation = 1.2 ÷ 1.5 = 80%. The shop can improve by standardising common repairs or booking appointments.

keyPoints: Process design sets the sequence and ownership of activities.
Capacity is limited by the bottleneck.
Utilisation = arrival rate ÷ capacity, and queues grow sharply as utilisation approaches 100%.
Little’s Law: WIP = throughput × flow time.
Quality is conformance to requirements and fitness for use, built into the process.
Lean removes waste through pull and flow; services add intangibility, simultaneity, variability and perishability.

en.title: Supply Chain Management
en.short: Coordination, forecasting, inventory, sourcing, logistics and the bullwhip effect.

sections.heading: Scope and trade-offs
sections.text: Supply chain management (SCM) plans and controls the flow of goods, information and money from suppliers to customers. It aims to match supply with demand at acceptable cost, service and resilience. Cost means total cost, not just purchase price. Service means availability, lead time and reliability. Resilience is the ability to recover from disruption. These goals conflict: more inventory improves service and resilience but raises holding cost; one low-cost supplier may be efficient but fragile.

sections.heading: Forecasting and bullwhip
sections.text: Demand forecasting predicts future demand from history and market signals. Forecast error is normal, so managers keep safety stock, extra inventory held as a buffer. The bullwhip effect is the widening of demand swings as orders move upstream. Causes include forecast updating, batch ordering, price promotions and rationing. Sharing point-of-sale data, shortening lead times and stable pricing reduce it. Coordination means aligning incentives and information across firms, for example through vendor managed inventory, where the supplier manages the buyer’s stock.

sections.heading: Inventory and EOQ
sections.text: Inventory includes raw materials, work in progress and finished goods. The economic order quantity (EOQ) balances ordering cost against holding cost. Formula: EOQ = √(2DS ÷ H), where D is annual demand, S is the cost per order and H is holding cost per unit per year. Example: D = 10,000 units, S = ₦500, H = ₦100. EOQ = √(2 × 10,000 × 500 ÷ 100) = √100,000 = 316 units, rounded. Orders per year = 10,000 ÷ 316 = 32, rounded. Total relevant cost = √(2DSH) = √(2 × 10,000 × 500 × 100) = ₦31,623 per year, rounded.

sections.heading: Sourcing and logistics
sections.text: Sourcing decides what to make or buy, how many suppliers to use and how to select them. Total cost of ownership includes price, quality, delivery and risk. Single sourcing gives scale and closeness but less resilience; multiple sourcing reduces risk but may raise cost. Logistics moves and stores goods through transport, warehousing and last-mile delivery. Coordination across these activities, with clear contracts and shared data, turns separate functions into a supply chain.

keyPoints: SCM balances total cost, service and resilience, and these goals conflict.
The bullwhip effect amplifies demand upstream; shared data and stable ordering reduce it.
EOQ = √(2DS ÷ H) balances ordering and holding costs.
The total relevant inventory cost at EOQ is √(2DSH) per year.
Sourcing choices trade price and scale against supply risk and total cost of ownership.
Logistics and coordination connect suppliers, operations and customers.

en.title: Organisational Behaviour and Managing People
en.short: Motivation, group dynamics, decision-making, power, culture and conflict in organisations.

sections.heading: Motivation at work
sections.text: Motivation explains why people choose effort and persist. Content theories such as Maslow’s hierarchy and Herzberg’s two-factor theory list needs or motivators. Herzberg’s two factors are hygiene factors, which prevent dissatisfaction, and motivators, which drive satisfaction. Process theories such as Vroom’s expectancy theory say effort depends on expectancy (will effort lead to performance?), instrumentality (will performance lead to reward?) and valence (how much the reward is valued). Equity theory adds fairness: workers compare their input-reward ratio with others. For managers, clear goals, fair rewards and feedback link motivation to performance.

sections.heading: Groups and teams
sections.text: A group is two or more people who interact and influence one another. Tuckman described forming, storming, norming and performing; adjourning was added later. Norms are shared rules, roles are expected behaviours, and cohesion is attraction to the group. Cohesion can raise performance but may also support groupthink, where pressure for agreement weakens critical thinking. Social loafing is reduced effort in a group. Clear tasks, accountability and diverse skills help teams perform.

sections.heading: Decision-making and power
sections.text: Managers rarely decide with perfect information. Bounded rationality means limits of information, time and attention; satisficing means choosing the first acceptable option. Biases include anchoring (over-reliance on first information), overconfidence and escalation of commitment, which is continuing a failing course. Power is the capacity to influence. French and Raven identified reward, coercive, legitimate, expert and referent bases. Organisational politics is the use of power to advance or protect interests. Politics can help change but can also raise conflict and cost.

sections.heading: Culture and conflict
sections.text: Culture is the shared assumptions, values and norms that guide behaviour. Schein described artefacts (visible signs such as layout and dress), espoused (stated) values and basic assumptions. A strong culture can coordinate people, but it can also exclude outsiders. Conflict is disagreement over interests, goals or values. Task conflict can improve decisions; relationship conflict usually harms them. Consider a Lagos logistics firm where sales and operations blamed each other for late deliveries. A joint weekly review clarified responsibilities and reduced blame. Managers should diagnose causes before choosing avoidance, compromise or collaboration.

keyPoints: Motivation depends on both valued rewards and the belief that effort will lead to performance.
Group norms, roles and cohesion shape team behaviour, and cohesion can produce groupthink.
Bounded rationality and cognitive biases mean managers often satisfice rather than optimise.
Power comes from several bases, and organisational politics is the use of power to advance or protect interests.
Culture is built from visible artefacts, espoused values and deeper assumptions.
Task conflict can improve decisions, while relationship conflict tends to damage performance.

en.title: Strategic Human Resource Management
en.short: Aligning workforce planning, recruitment, performance, reward, talent and employee relations with strategy.

sections.heading: Strategy and fit
sections.text: Strategic human resource management (SHRM) means designing HR policies so they support the organisation’s strategy and help it perform. Vertical fit is alignment between HR practice and business strategy; horizontal fit is consistency among HR practices, such as recruitment, appraisal and reward. The resource-based view argues that people can support sustained advantage when their skills are valuable, rare and hard to copy. A cost-focused firm and a service-focused firm therefore need different workforce plans, appraisal criteria and pay systems.

sections.heading: Planning and selection
sections.text: Workforce planning forecasts how many people, with which skills, the strategy needs, then compares this with likely supply. Demand comes from workload and plans; supply comes from current staff, turnover and internal moves. Suppose a firm needs 120 technicians next year. It has 100, expects 10 leavers and 5 internal promotions into technician roles. Available staff = 100 − 10 + 5 = 95, so external hires needed = 120 − 95 = 25. Recruitment attracts candidates; selection chooses among them. Structured interviews and work samples are generally more reliable than unstructured interviews. A selection ratio is hires divided by applicants.

sections.heading: Performance, reward and relations
sections.text: Performance management sets goals, gives feedback, appraises results and plans development. It should measure what strategy values, not only what is easy to count. Reward includes pay, benefits and non-financial recognition. It must be internally fair and externally competitive, and pay for performance can encourage short-term behaviour if badly designed. Talent management identifies critical roles and develops successors. Employee relations covers voice, grievance handling, collective bargaining (union negotiation over pay and conditions) and engagement. Employment law and union rules differ by country, so managers must check the local framework. A retailer moving to premium service should include customer satisfaction in appraisal and reward, not sales volume alone.

keyPoints: SHRM aligns HR practices with strategy (vertical fit) and with each other (horizontal fit).
Workforce planning compares forecast demand with forecast supply to find the gap.
External hires needed = demand − (current staff − leavers + internal moves).
Recruitment attracts applicants; selection chooses among them, preferably with structured methods.
Reward must balance internal fairness, external competitiveness and strategic behaviour.
Talent management and employee relations support retention and voice; employment law varies by country.

en.title: Leadership and Organisational Change
en.short: Leadership theories, culture, change models and resistance, and how to lead planned change.

sections.heading: Leadership and influence
sections.text: Leadership is influencing others towards shared goals. Trait theories look for personal qualities. Behavioural theories study what leaders do, such as concern for tasks and people. Contingency theories say the best style depends on the situation. Transformational leaders raise motivation through a vision and individual support; transactional leaders rely on rewards and correction. Influence also rests on power bases: legitimate, reward, coercive, expert and referent. Expert and referent power usually last longer because they do not depend on formal rank.

sections.heading: Culture
sections.text: Organisational culture is the shared pattern of values, beliefs and behaviour. Edgar Schein describes three levels: artefacts, the visible symbols and routines; espoused values, what people say they believe; and basic assumptions, the deep, taken-for-granted beliefs. Culture decides whether a change looks normal or threatening. Leaders can diagnose culture and align stories, rewards and symbols with the change, but deep assumptions change slowly.

sections.heading: Change models
sections.text: Kurt Lewin described unfreezing, changing and refreezing. John Kotter offers eight steps: create urgency, build a coalition, form a vision, communicate it, remove barriers, win short-term gains, consolidate, and embed the change. Resistance is normal. People resist when they fear losing competence, status or security, or when they do not trust the case. Leaders should listen, explain, involve affected staff, offer support and run a pilot.

sections.heading: Leading planned change
sections.text: In a made-up case, Ngozi leads a 120-person packaging firm in Ogun State. She wants digital job cards. She builds a coalition, explains the reason, trains supervisors and pilots one line. Two supervisors resist because they fear losing control of records. She involves them in designing the form and keeps a paper backup for a month. Resistance falls and the change spreads.

keyPoints: Leadership is influence towards shared goals, not only formal authority.
Contingency theories say effective leadership depends on the situation.
French and Raven’s five power bases are legitimate, reward, coercive, expert and referent.
Schein’s culture levels are artefacts, espoused values and basic assumptions.
Lewin’s model is unfreeze, change and refreeze; Kotter gives eight steps.
Resistance is normal, so involve people, communicate and support them.

en.title: Business Ethics and Corporate Governance
en.short: Ethical theories, stakeholder analysis, codes of conduct, board duties and governance failures.

sections.heading: Ethical frameworks
sections.text: Ethics asks what a manager ought to do. Consequentialism judges an act by its outcomes; utilitarianism seeks the greatest good for the greatest number. Deontology judges acts by duties and rules, such as telling the truth whatever the result. Virtue ethics asks what a person of good character would do, stressing honesty and courage. Justice theories examine fair distribution of benefits and burdens. These frameworks often conflict, so a manager should state the facts, identify the values at stake and test the decision from more than one view.

sections.heading: Stakeholders and codes
sections.text: Stakeholder analysis identifies everyone affected by or affecting a decision: owners, employees, customers, suppliers, lenders, communities and regulators. Map each stakeholder’s power, interest and legitimacy, then decide who must be consulted and who must be informed. A code of conduct states expected behaviour, such as avoiding bribes and conflicts of interest. It only works if leaders model it, training is real and breaches are punished. Codes are not law, though regulators may require firms to have one; they guide judgement.

sections.heading: Boards and accountability
sections.text: The board oversees management on behalf of shareholders and the company. Its roles include setting strategy, approving budgets and major transactions, appointing and monitoring the chief executive, ensuring reliable reporting and managing risk. Directors owe fiduciary duties of care and loyalty: act honestly, in the company’s interest, and avoid conflicts. Accountability means explaining decisions to owners and, in many countries, to regulators and the public. An agency problem arises when managers’ interests differ from owners'; independent directors, audit committees and external audit are checks, though none is perfect.

sections.heading: Governance failure case
sections.text: A fictional Lagos food company, Adeyemi Foods, gave a supply contract to a director’s brother. The audit committee saw the conflict but did not act. A junior buyer who objected was ignored. Eventually quality fell and a lender withdrew support. The failure lay in board independence, whistleblowing and tone at the top, the ethical example leaders set, not in missing rules. Analysis should ask: who benefited, who was harmed, which duty was breached and which control failed?

keyPoints: Consequentialism judges outcomes, deontology judges duties, and virtue ethics judges character.
Stakeholder analysis maps power, interest and legitimacy to decide consultation.
A code of conduct guides behaviour but needs leadership, training and enforcement.
Directors owe fiduciary duties of care and loyalty and must manage conflicts.
Accountability requires explaining decisions to owners and other affected parties.
Governance failures often lie in board independence, incentives and culture, not only missing rules.

en.title: Business law and compliance for managers
en.short: Contracts, agency, company and employment law, competition, consumer protection and compliance.

sections.heading: Contracts and agency
sections.text: A contract is a legally enforceable agreement. It usually needs offer, acceptance, consideration (something of value exchanged), intention to create legal relations and capacity. Managers should record terms clearly and know when liability begins. Agency is a relationship where an agent acts for a principal. The agent needs authority, either actual (express or implied) or apparent, and owes fiduciary duties such as loyalty and disclosure. An agent who exceeds authority may bind the principal or become personally liable, depending on the law. Statutes and case law vary by country, so check local rules.

sections.heading: Company and employment law
sections.text: Company law basics include incorporation, separate legal personality and limited liability. A company owns assets and contracts in its own name; shareholders normally risk only their investment. Directors owe duties of care, loyalty and good faith. Employment law principles cover the contract of employment, employee versus independent contractor status, pay, working time, termination, discrimination and health and safety. Many protections are mandatory and cannot be waived. Rules differ by country and sometimes by state or province, so confirm the current statute and regulator guidance.

sections.heading: Competition, consumers, compliance
sections.text: Competition law usually prohibits anti-competitive agreements, abuse of dominance and mergers that substantially lessen competition. Consumer protection law addresses misleading claims, product safety, fair terms and redress. Compliance means the systems a firm uses to meet legal and regulatory duties: risk assessment, policies, training, monitoring, record keeping and whistleblowing channels. It is preventive, not just legal advice after a dispute. Penalties can include fines, damages and disqualification.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: Amina manages a Nairobi wholesaler. A sales agent orders stock beyond the agent’s written authority. The supplier may still enforce the contract against the firm if apparent authority applies, but Amina should review controls. Separately, a director signs a personal guarantee, so limited liability may not protect him. The firm must also check employment contracts, competition rules and consumer complaints under Kenyan law, not assume Nigerian or UK rules apply.

keyPoints: A contract usually needs offer, acceptance, consideration, intention and capacity.
An agent needs authority and owes the principal fiduciary duties.
A company has separate legal personality, while directors owe duties of care and loyalty.
Employment protections are often mandatory but vary by country.
Competition law targets anti-competitive conduct, and consumer law targets misleading or unsafe practices.
Compliance is a preventive system of risk assessment, policies, training and monitoring.

en.title: Business Analytics and Data-Driven Decisions
en.short: Descriptive statistics, probability, sampling, hypothesis tests, regression and predictive analytics for managers.

sections.heading: From data to decisions
sections.text: Descriptive statistics summarise data. The mean is the average; the median is the middle value; the mode is the most frequent. Range and standard deviation measure spread. Ask how data were collected: biased samples, missing values and survivorship bias mislead. Correlation does not prove causation.

sections.heading: Probability and sampling
sections.text: Probability is the chance of an event, from 0 to 1. Expected value is the sum of each outcome multiplied by its probability. Sampling studies a subset. Random sampling reduces selection bias. The standard error of a mean is s ÷ √n, where s is the sample standard deviation and n the sample size. Larger samples give smaller standard errors. A confidence interval gives a range likely to contain the true value.

sections.heading: Testing and regression
sections.text: A hypothesis test compares a null hypothesis with data. The p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme if the null is true. A small p-value, often below 0.05, is evidence against the null; 0.05 is a convention, not a law. Regression fits y = a + bx. The slope b is the change in y per unit change in x. R² is the share of variation explained. Test predictive models on new data to avoid overfitting.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Sales in thousand units are 10, 12, 14, 16, 18. Mean = 70 ÷ 5 = 14. Median = 14. Sample standard deviation = √(40 ÷ 4) = 3.16. Standard error = 3.16 ÷ √5 = 1.41. Test H0: mean = 12 against mean > 12: t = (14 − 12) ÷ 1.41 = 1.42. With 4 degrees of freedom, the 5% one-tailed critical t is about 2.13, so the result is not significant. Regression for x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 10, 12, 14, 16 gives y = 8 + 2x; at x = 5, predicted y = 18. Avoid bias, misreading p-values and overfitting.

keyPoints: Descriptive statistics summarise centre and spread; always check how the data were collected.
Expected value = Σ(outcome × probability), and standard error = s ÷ √n.
Random sampling reduces bias, and larger samples reduce standard error.
A small p-value is evidence against the null, not the probability the null is true; 0.05 is only a convention.
In y = a + bx, b is the change in y per unit change in x; R² is the share of variation explained.
Validate predictive models on new data and do not confuse correlation with causation.

en.title: Information Systems and Digital Transformation
en.short: Information systems, databases, enterprise systems, cybersecurity, platforms and digital business models.

sections.heading: Systems and data
sections.text:
An information system combines people, processes, data and technology to collect, store and use information. A database is an organised collection of data; a database management system (DBMS) controls access and integrity. Relational databases store data in tables linked by keys and are queried with SQL, a standard query language.

Enterprise systems integrate functions across the firm. Enterprise resource planning (ERP) shares one database for finance, inventory and production. Customer relationship management (CRM) tracks customers, and supply chain management (SCM) systems coordinate suppliers. Integration improves visibility but raises implementation cost and change-management risk.

sections.heading: Cybersecurity and governance
sections.text:
Cybersecurity protects systems and data from unauthorised access, damage and disruption. The CIA triad names confidentiality, integrity and availability. Controls include authentication, access rights, encryption, backups, patching and incident response. Risk is managed by identifying threats and vulnerabilities, then reducing likelihood or impact. Laws on data protection differ by country; managers must check the local rules.

IT governance sets decision rights and accountability for technology. Frameworks such as COBIT help align IT with strategy and monitor risk. Governance also covers vendor contracts, data ownership and audit trails.

sections.heading: Platforms and models
sections.text:
A platform creates value by connecting two or more groups, such as buyers and sellers. Network effects mean the platform becomes more useful as more users join. This can create winner-takes-most competition, so governance of access, pricing and data becomes strategic.

Digital business models include subscription, advertising, transaction fees and freemium (free basic service, paid extras). Digital transformation is the redesign of operations, customer experience and business models using technology. It changes competition by lowering some costs and raising the value of data and ecosystems.

sections.heading: Case: M-Pesa
sections.text: M-Pesa, launched by Safaricom in Kenya in 2007, is a mobile money platform. It links customers, agents and merchants. Its value grew as more users and agents joined. It changed payments, and it forced banks and regulators to respond. The lesson is that technology creates value only when processes, trust and rules adapt with it.

keyPoints: An information system is people, processes, data and technology working together.
Databases and enterprise systems improve integration but require data discipline and change management.
Cybersecurity balances confidentiality, integrity and availability through layered controls.
IT governance assigns decision rights and accountability for technology and data.
Platforms grow through network effects, which can create winner-takes-most markets.
Digital transformation changes operations, competition and governance, not just technology.

en.title: Strategic Management: Analysis, Choice and Execution
en.short: External and internal analysis, competitive advantage, business-level strategy, and putting strategy into action.

sections.heading: Outside the firm
sections.text: PESTEL scans the macro environment: political, economic, social, technological, environmental and legal factors. It widens attention but does not show profit potential. Michael Porter’s five forces framework does: rivalry among existing firms, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of buyers and bargaining power of suppliers. Strong forces squeeze returns. A manager asks which forces are changing and why.

sections.heading: Inside the firm
sections.text: Internal analysis asks what the firm can do. The value chain splits activities into primary activities such as inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, and service, and support activities such as procurement, technology and human resources. It helps locate where cost or differentiation is created. The resource-based view looks for resources that are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and well organised. SWOT then combines strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats, but it is only a summary; it must lead to choices, not a long list.

sections.heading: Competitive advantage
sections.text: A firm has competitive advantage when it creates more value than rivals or does so at lower cost. Business-level strategy chooses how to compete in one market. Porter’s generic strategies are cost leadership, differentiation and focus, which serves a narrow segment. A firm can pursue a hybrid, but it risks being stuck in the middle, with no clear cost or differentiation advantage. Advantage must be durable: imitation, substitution and changing customer needs erode it.

sections.heading: Formulation and delivery
sections.text: Formulation sets mission, objectives and the chosen position. Implementation turns it into structure, budgets, incentives, processes and culture. A plan fails if resources and rewards do not fit it. Suppose Ada runs a fictional Lagos food company. PESTEL shows rising fuel costs; five forces show strong buyer power. Her value chain shows cold storage is costly. She chooses focus differentiation: fresh, reliable meals for offices, supported by a small delivery fleet and staff bonuses for on-time delivery. SWOT confirms the fit, and monthly reviews test it.

keyPoints: PESTEL scans macro factors; five forces explains industry profit pressure.
The value chain locates cost and differentiation; the resource-based view tests whether advantage can last.
Competitive advantage is superior value or lower cost, and it must survive imitation.
Porter’s generic strategies are cost leadership, differentiation and focus.
Formulation chooses a position; implementation aligns structure, budgets, incentives and culture.
SWOT is only a summary and should end in choices.

en.title: Corporate strategy, growth and acquisitions
en.short: Diversification, vertical integration, M&A, alliances, portfolio choices and parenting advantage.

sections.heading: Growth choices
sections.text: Corporate strategy asks how a multi-business firm should be more than the sum of its parts. Diversification means entering new products and new markets. Related diversification shares capabilities or resources; unrelated diversification, often called a conglomerate, shares little. Vertical integration means owning a neighbouring stage: backward into suppliers, or forward into distribution. It can reduce transaction costs and secure supply, but it raises fixed costs and reduces flexibility. Diversification can spread risk, but it can also blur accountability and subsidise weak units. It must show where the parent adds value.

sections.heading: Mergers and alliances
sections.text: Mergers and acquisitions (M&A) combine two firms or buy another firm outright. Synergy is the extra value from combining them. The acquisition premium is the amount paid above the target’s standalone value. A deal creates value only if synergy exceeds the premium and integration costs. Alliances, such as joint ventures, share risk and knowledge without full ownership, but control and exit are harder.

sections.heading: Portfolio and parenting
sections.text: Portfolio decisions allocate capital across businesses. Tools such as the growth-share matrix (the BCG matrix) classify units, but they do not decide by themselves. Parenting advantage means the corporate parent adds more value to a business than another owner would. Parents create value through coaching, central services and capital discipline. They destroy it through bureaucracy, slow decisions, cross-subsidy and weak performance rules.

sections.heading: Worked case
sections.text: Kano Foods buys a packaging firm. The target’s standalone value is ₦500m and expected synergy is ₦150m. Kano pays ₦600m. Net value = 500 + 150 − 600 = ₦50m, so the deal adds value, ignoring integration costs for simplicity. If synergy were only ₦80m, net value = 500 + 80 − 600 = −₦20m, destroying value. The premium and integration costs must be tested carefully.

keyPoints: Corporate strategy is about making the multi-business firm worth more than its separate units.
Related diversification shares resources; unrelated diversification shares little and needs strong parenting.
Vertical integration can secure supply or distribution but raises fixed costs and reduces flexibility.
M&A creates value only when synergy exceeds the premium and integration costs.
Alliances share risk and knowledge but weaken control.
Net acquisition value = standalone value + synergy − price paid; parenting advantage means the parent adds more value than another owner.

en.title: International Business and Global Strategy
en.short: Globalisation, market entry, institutions, currency exposure and global organisation.

sections.heading: Globalisation and strategy
sections.text: Globalisation means growing cross-border flows of goods, capital, people and information. Firms internationalise to reach markets, gain resources, lower costs or learn. A global strategy is the plan for how a firm configures and adapts activities such as production, marketing and research across countries. The integration-responsiveness framework sets global integration, which favours scale and standardisation, against local responsiveness, which favours adaptation to tastes and regulation. A transnational strategy seeks both through shared systems and local units.

sections.heading: Entry and institutions
sections.text: Entry modes include exporting, licensing, franchising, joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries. Each trades control against risk, capital and speed. Cultural differences cover language, values and behaviour; Hofstede’s dimensions are a debated framework. Institutional differences include formal rules such as law and tax, and informal norms. Institutional voids exist where reliable intermediaries, credit or courts are weak. Managers adapt product, pricing and employment practices to local conditions; ethics needs judgement rather than simple adaptation. Example: a Kenyan dairy firm entering Uganda may export first, then license a local processor before building a plant.

sections.heading: Trade and currency exposure
sections.text: Tariffs, quotas and rules of origin shape trade access. Foreign exchange exposure has three forms: transaction exposure on known foreign-currency cash flows, translation exposure in consolidated accounts, and economic exposure to future competitiveness. A forward fixes a future rate. Made-up example: a Nigerian exporter expects US$100,000 in 90 days. The forward rate is ₦1,600/$. If the spot rate at settlement is ₦1,500/$, the unhedged receipt is ₦150,000,000, while the forward gives ₦160,000,000, a gain of ₦10,000,000. If spot rose to ₦1,700/$, the forward would give up ₦10,000,000. Hedging reduces uncertainty; it does not guarantee a better outcome than staying unhedged.

sections.heading: Global organisation
sections.text: Global structures include international division, global product, global area and matrix forms. Product structures support global brands and scale; area structures support local responsiveness; a matrix balances both but can blur accountability. Coordination uses shared values, global teams, expatriate managers and transfer pricing, the prices set for transactions between units of the same firm. Transfer prices must follow tax rules. Control systems should reward integration and local learning.

keyPoints: Global strategy balances pressures for global integration and local responsiveness.
Entry mode choice trades control against risk, capital and speed.
Cultural and institutional differences require adaptation, not one universal model.
Transaction exposure affects known foreign-currency cash flows; translation and economic exposure also matter.
Forward receipt = foreign currency amount × forward rate; hedging reduces uncertainty but can mean forgoing gains.
Global structures and transfer pricing must fit strategy and comply with tax rules.

en.title: Entrepreneurship and Innovation Management
en.short: Opportunity recognition, business models, lean start-up, innovation portfolios and scaling.

sections.heading: Opportunity and business models
sections.text:
Opportunity recognition is the disciplined search for a problem that customers will pay to solve. An idea becomes an opportunity only when a viable business model exists. A business model describes how a venture creates, delivers and captures value. Its core is the value proposition (what the customer gets and why they pay), the customer segment, the revenue model and the cost structure.

Tools such as the Business Model Canvas help teams map these elements on one page. Established firms also need to renew their models, not just their products, because digital technology can make old models obsolete.

sections.heading: Lean start-up
sections.text:
The lean start-up method, popularised by Eric Ries, treats a new venture as a series of experiments. Build a minimum viable product (MVP), the smallest version that lets you test your key assumption with real customers.

Measure their behaviour, learn whether the assumptions hold, then decide to persevere or pivot. A pivot is a structured change of strategy while keeping what has been learned. This reduces the waste of building something nobody wants. Large firms use the same logic in corporate innovation labs.

sections.heading: Innovation portfolios and scaling
sections.text:
An innovation portfolio balances incremental improvements, adjacent extensions and radical bets. Ambidexterity is the ability to exploit today’s business while exploring tomorrow’s. Portfolio reviews should kill weak projects early and redirect funds.

Scaling means growing revenue faster than costs. Unit economics are the profit earned on one customer. A made-up example: a firm spends ₦120,000 on sales and marketing and gains 40 customers, so customer acquisition cost (CAC) is ₦3,000. Each customer yields ₦600 monthly gross profit and stays 20 months, so lifetime value (LTV) is ₦12,000. LTV:CAC is 4, and payback is 5 months. Healthy unit economics like these support scaling; poor ones make growth destroy cash.

keyPoints: An opportunity is an idea with a viable business model, not just a product concept.
A business model explains how a venture creates, delivers and captures value.
Lean start-up uses build-measure-learn cycles and minimum viable products to test assumptions and pivot.
CAC = sales and marketing spend ÷ customers acquired; LTV = monthly gross profit × average customer lifetime.
Payback period = CAC ÷ monthly gross profit; a common rough guide is LTV:CAC above 3, but norms vary by industry.
Innovation portfolios balance incremental, adjacent and radical projects; scaling requires healthy unit economics.

en.title: Project Management: Planning, Control and Agile Delivery
en.short: Selecting, scoping, scheduling, costing, risk and stakeholder control, with agile delivery.

sections.heading: Selection and scope
sections.text:
A project is a temporary, unique effort with a defined outcome. Selection compares strategic fit, benefits, risk and financial return, using scoring models or discounted cash flow; test the assumptions.

Scope states deliverables and boundaries. A project charter authorises the work. A work breakdown structure (WBS) divides deliverables into work packages. Scope creep is uncontrolled change; change control assesses its impact before approval.

sections.heading: Scheduling and cost
sections.text:
Scheduling sequences activities, estimates durations and dependencies. The critical path is the longest dependent path; it sets the minimum duration, and delay on it delays the project. Gantt charts show timing.

The cost baseline is the approved budget by period. Earned value management (EVM) compares planned value (PV), earned value (EV) and actual cost (AC). Example: PV ₦100,000, EV ₦80,000, AC ₦90,000. Schedule variance = EV − PV = −₦20,000, so work is behind schedule. Cost variance = EV − AC = −₦10,000, so it is over budget. CPI = EV ÷ AC = 0.889; SPI = EV ÷ PV = 0.80.

sections.heading: Risk and stakeholders
sections.text:
Risk is an uncertain event that may affect objectives. A risk register records each risk, its probability, impact, owner and response: avoid, reduce, transfer or accept.

Stakeholders are people or groups affected by or able to affect the project. A power-interest grid prioritises engagement, and a communication plan sets what is shared, with whom and when.

sections.heading: Agile delivery
sections.text:
Agile delivery uses short iterations, cross-functional teams and customer feedback, with planning adjusted as learning grows.

In Scrum, a product backlog lists desired work; sprints are fixed short periods; daily stand-ups coordinate; sprint reviews show increments; retrospectives improve process. Agile suits uncertain scope; predictive planning suits stable or regulated work. Hybrid approaches combine both.

keyPoints: A project is temporary and unique; its charter authorises it and the WBS defines scope.
The critical path is the longest dependent path and sets the shortest possible duration.
Schedule variance = EV − PV; cost variance = EV − AC.
CPI = EV ÷ AC and SPI = EV ÷ PV; below 1 means over budget or behind schedule.
Risk responses are avoid, reduce, transfer and accept, each with an owner.
Agile uses short iterations and feedback, and suits uncertain scope.

en.title: Negotiation and Conflict Resolution
en.short: Distributive and integrative bargaining, preparation, persuasion and dispute resolution.

sections.heading: Two bargaining logics
sections.text: Distributive negotiation treats the issue as a fixed pie: one side’s gain is the other’s loss, so each tries to claim value. Integrative negotiation looks for trades across issues so both sides can create value. It works when parties have different priorities, not necessarily different goals. Skilled negotiators often mix both: create value first, then claim a fair share. Conflict is not always bad; task conflict can improve decisions, while personal conflict harms trust.

sections.heading: Preparation and the ZOPA
sections.text: Preparation means diagnosing interests, not just positions. A position is what a party says it wants; an interest is why. Each side needs a BATNA, the best alternative to a negotiated agreement. The reservation price is the least favourable deal acceptable given that BATNA. The zone of possible agreement (ZOPA) is the range between the parties’ reservation prices. A made-up case: Ngozi sells cartons to a Lagos food company. Her reservation is ₦900; the buyer’s is ₦1,100. The ZOPA is ₦900 to ₦1,100. If their reservation prices do not overlap, no deal is rational unless the alternatives change.

sections.heading: Bargaining and persuasion
sections.text: Bargaining opens with anchors, offers and concessions. An anchor is the first number put on the table, and it pulls the final deal toward it. Concessions should be reciprocal and shrinking. Persuasion rests on credibility, clear framing and listening. Framing presents the same facts as a gain or a loss, and people often react differently. In integrative talks, ask about priorities and offer packages rather than single numbers.

sections.heading: Resolving disputes
sections.text: When talks stall, dispute resolution moves from negotiation to mediation, where a neutral third party helps but cannot impose a settlement, then to arbitration, where a third party decides and the award is often binding, and finally to litigation in court. Mediation preserves relationships and is usually cheaper; arbitration offers privacy and expertise. Choose according to enforceability, cost, time and the need to preserve the relationship.

keyPoints: Distributive negotiation claims value from a fixed pie; integrative negotiation creates value through trades.
BATNA is the best alternative to a negotiated agreement and sets your reservation price.
The ZOPA is the range between the parties’ reservation prices; no overlap means no rational deal.
Prepare by moving from positions to interests.
Persuasion depends on credibility, framing and listening; concessions should be reciprocal.
Mediation aids settlement; arbitration decides and is often binding; litigation is the court route.

en.title: Enterprise Risk Management
en.short: Risk identification, assessment, appetite, mitigation, internal control and continuity in decisions.

sections.heading: Risk and appetite
sections.text:
Enterprise risk management (ERM) is a structured way to identify, assess and manage uncertainty affecting objectives. Risk is the effect of uncertainty on objectives; it may be a threat or an opportunity. Identification uses workshops, interviews, process maps and scenario analysis, recorded in a risk register with owners.

Assessment rates likelihood and impact, first as inherent risk before controls and then as residual risk after controls. Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk the board will accept; risk tolerance sets limits within it. A clear appetite statement guides decisions.

sections.heading: Mitigation and control
sections.text:
Mitigation chooses a response: avoid the activity, reduce likelihood or impact, transfer or share risk through insurance or contracts, or accept it. Internal control is the policies and procedures giving reasonable assurance of reliable reporting, effective operations and compliance.

Preventive controls stop errors; detective controls find them. Examples are segregation of duties, authorisation limits, reconciliations and IT access controls. The three lines model separates management ownership, a risk and compliance function, and independent internal audit. Key risk indicators (KRIs) warn when risk is rising.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Worked example. A made-up firm faces supplier failure with 20% annual probability and $500,000 impact. Expected loss = 0.20 × 500,000 = $100,000.

A $30,000 mitigation plan cuts probability to 8%. Residual expected loss = 0.08 × 500,000 = $40,000. Total expected cost with mitigation = 30,000 + 40,000 = $70,000. The saving is 100,000 − 70,000 = $30,000, so the plan is worth considering if estimates are sound.

sections.heading: Continuity and decisions
sections.text:
Business continuity management prepares for disruption. A business impact analysis identifies critical activities and sets recovery time objectives (RTO), the maximum acceptable downtime, and recovery point objectives (RPO), the maximum acceptable data loss.

Plans need testing and updating. ERM supports decisions by placing risk beside return: project approvals, pricing, capital allocation and supplier choices use residual risk and appetite limits. ISO 31000 and COSO ERM are frameworks; regulation may add requirements, so check current rules.

keyPoints: ERM identifies, assesses and manages uncertainty that affects objectives, treating risk as a threat or an opportunity.
Risk appetite is the risk the board accepts; tolerance sets limits within it.
Mitigation responses are avoid, reduce, transfer or share, and accept.
Internal control uses preventive and detective controls such as segregation of duties and authorisation limits.
Expected loss = probability × impact; compare residual expected loss plus control cost with the original expected loss.
Business continuity uses a business impact analysis to set RTO and RPO, and plans must be tested.

en.title: Sustainability and ESG in Business
en.short: Environmental and social impacts, ESG measurement and reporting, and evaluating sustainability trade-offs.

sections.heading: Impacts and stakeholders
sections.text: Sustainability means meeting present needs without compromising future generations (Brundtland Commission, 1987). Environmental impacts include emissions, water, waste and biodiversity; social impacts include labour rights, health and safety and community effects. These are externalities when costs fall on others. Stakeholder theory, associated with Edward Freeman, says a firm answers to everyone affected, not only shareholders. Expectations vary by country and sector. Materiality means issues significant enough to affect decisions. Double materiality has two sides: financial materiality, how sustainability affects the firm, and impact materiality, how the firm affects people and the planet. The EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive requires double materiality; rules differ elsewhere.

sections.heading: ESG measurement and reporting
sections.text: ESG stands for environmental, social and governance. It is a framework for assessing performance, not a single score. Measurement is difficult: data gaps, estimates and different rating methods mean agencies often disagree. Reporting standards also differ. GRI (Global Reporting Initiative) focuses on impacts on the economy, environment and people. The ISSB (International Sustainability Standards Board) issued IFRS S1 and S2 in 2023 as a global baseline for investor-focused reporting; TCFD (Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures) climate disclosures are now taken forward by the ISSB. The EU CSRD is broader. Assurance by an independent provider adds credibility. Always check which rules apply in your country and year.

sections.heading: Models and trade-offs
sections.text: Sustainable business models aim to create value while reducing harm. A circular economy keeps materials in use through repair, reuse and recycling. Product-as-a-service sells access rather than ownership, so the maker keeps responsibility for the product. Renewable energy and supply chain changes cut emissions. Trade-offs are unavoidable. A made-up Lagos firm can pay ₦8,000,000 extra for a cleaner boiler that saves ₦2,000,000 a year in fuel. Payback = 8,000,000 ÷ 2,000,000 = 4 years. If the board requires 3 years, the project fails the financial test but cuts emissions. The board must weigh the strategic and regulatory benefits against the wait.

keyPoints: Sustainability covers environmental and social impacts, including externalities that fall on others.
Stakeholder expectations and materiality decide which issues a firm must manage.
ESG is a measurement and reporting framework, not one reliable score.
GRI reports impacts, while ISSB IFRS S1 and S2 provide an investor-focused global baseline.
Double materiality combines financial materiality and impact materiality.
Payback = extra cost ÷ annual savings, a simple test that exposes sustainability trade-offs.

en.title: Managerial Communication and Persuasion
en.short: It covers audience analysis, clear writing and speaking, persuasion, feedback and cross-cultural communication.

sections.heading: Audience and purpose
sections.text: Managerial communication is how managers exchange information and meaning to coordinate work and influence decisions. It starts with audience analysis: who will read or hear the message, what they know, what they need, and what concerns or authority they have. A message to a finance director and a message to a shift team serve different purposes. Define the purpose in one sentence: inform, request action, persuade or record a decision. Then choose the channel, such as email, report, meeting or face-to-face talk. The channel should fit urgency, complexity and the need for discussion.

sections.heading: Writing and speaking
sections.text: Written communication should be clear, concise and structured. Put the main point early, use short paragraphs and headings, and state the action you want. Plain language reduces misunderstanding, especially for second-language readers. Oral communication adds tone, pace and body language. Prepare an opening, two or three main points and a close that asks for a decision. Listening is part of speaking: pause, check understanding and note objections. In meetings, a chairperson should keep time, invite quieter members and summarise decisions.

sections.heading: Persuasion and feedback
sections.text: Persuasion means influencing belief or action through credible reasoning and emotion. Aristotle described three appeals: ethos (the speaker’s credibility), pathos (the audience’s feelings) and logos (logic and evidence). A manager builds ethos by being honest and prepared, uses logos with facts, and pathos with a human consequence. Feedback should be timely, specific and focused on behaviour, not personality. Ask the receiver to paraphrase the message. This closes the loop and shows whether meaning was shared.

sections.heading: Cross-cultural case
sections.text: Cross-cultural communication means adjusting to differences in directness, formality, hierarchy and silence. Avoid stereotypes; ask about preferences. In Lagos, Ngozi, an operations manager, must persuade branch managers to adopt a new stock process. She analyses their concerns, sends a one-page memo with evidence, presents at a meeting and invites feedback. She also offers face-to-face briefings for staff who prefer discussion. The result is a shared decision, not a one-way order.

keyPoints: Start every message by defining the purpose and analysing the audience.
Written messages should put the main point early and state the action required.
Oral communication needs structure, delivery and active listening.
Aristotle’s ethos, pathos and logos describe credibility, emotion and logic in persuasion.
Useful feedback is timely, specific and focused on behaviour, and the receiver should paraphrase it.
Cross-cultural communication requires adapting to differences without stereotyping.

en.title: Research Methods for Business Decisions
en.short: Research design, literature review, qualitative and quantitative methods, sampling, validity and ethics.

sections.heading: Design and questions
sections.text:
Research design is the plan that links a question to evidence. It states the purpose, the unit of analysis (the level studied, such as a customer or firm), the data needed and how they will be collected and analysed. A good design starts with a clear question, not a method. Exploratory studies ask what is happening; descriptive studies measure it; explanatory studies test causes. A hypothesis is a testable statement about a relationship between variables. A variable is any characteristic that can take different values.

A design also sets boundaries. It says what will be studied, what will not, and how bias will be reduced. The choice depends on the question, the time available and access to data.

sections.heading: Literature and methods
sections.text: A literature review summarises what is known, groups the main debates and identifies a gap. It is not a list of summaries. Use it to sharpen the question and choose concepts. Quantitative methods collect numbers and test hypotheses with statistics; qualitative methods collect words, images or observations and explore meaning. Common qualitative approaches include interviews, focus groups and case studies. Mixed methods combine both. Each method has limits, so explain why it fits the question.

sections.heading: Sampling and validity
sections.text: Sampling selects part of a population to represent the whole. In probability sampling every member has a known chance of selection; examples are simple random, systematic and stratified sampling. In non-probability sampling, such as convenience sampling, the chance is unknown, so generalisation is weak. A sampling frame is the list from which the sample is drawn. Validity means the study measures what it claims. Internal validity concerns cause and effect; external validity concerns generalisation. Reliability means consistent results on repetition. Triangulation checks a finding against another source or method.

sections.heading: Ethics and a case
sections.text:
Ethics requires informed consent, meaning participants understand and freely agree, plus confidentiality, anonymity and care to avoid harm. Researchers must seek approval from an ethics committee and store data securely.

In a case, a Lagos retailer wants to know why customers wait. It interviews ten customers and times 200 visits chosen by systematic sampling. Interviews explain feelings; timings measure delay. If lunchtime visits are timed, external validity is weak.

keyPoints: Start with a clear research question and let it drive the design.
A literature review groups debates and identifies a gap; it is not a list of summaries.
Quantitative methods test hypotheses with numbers; qualitative methods explore meaning.
Probability sampling gives every member a known chance of selection; non-probability sampling does not.
For systematic sampling, interval = population size ÷ sample size.
Validity concerns measuring what you claim; reliability concerns consistency; ethics requires consent, confidentiality and no harm.

en.title: Business Policy and Integrative Decision-Making
en.short: This summary combines functional views into one strategic decision, covering fit, stakeholders and uncertainty.

sections.heading: The capstone question
sections.text: Business policy is the top-level process of choosing what the whole firm should do and how its parts should support that choice. An integrative decision combines the functional views you have studied: marketing, finance, operations, people and law. Strategic fit has two sides. Internal fit means the choices are consistent with one another, so a growth promise is matched by capacity and cash. External fit means they match the market, regulation and other outside conditions. A capstone case asks for one reasoned decision, not a set of separate departmental answers.

sections.heading: Stakeholders and trade-offs
sections.text: Stakeholders are people or groups affected by a decision, such as owners, employees, customers, suppliers, lenders, communities and regulators. A trade-off means gaining one thing by giving up another. Integrative judgement does not maximise one stakeholder’s interest blindly. It identifies who is materially affected, what each needs, and which constraints are legal, ethical or contractual. It then chooses and explains the balance. A decision that pleases shareholders but destroys employee trust or breaches a permit is rarely sustainable.

sections.heading: Case analysis and example
sections.text: Case analysis follows a discipline: state the decision issue, list options, set criteria, analyse evidence, decide, then plan implementation. Under uncertainty, use scenario ranges, pilot tests and stage gates, where spending is released only after a review. A made-up example: Kemi’s food firm must expand. Option A is a large loan-financed plant; option B is a staged plant with a pilot line. Criteria and weights are financial risk 0.4, strategic fit 0.3 and stakeholder impact 0.3. Scores from 1 to 5, where 5 is best: A scores 3, 4, 3, giving 1.2 + 1.2 + 0.9 = 3.3. B scores 4, 3, 4, giving 1.6 + 0.9 + 1.2 = 3.7. B ranks higher, but Kemi must test demand and cash assumptions before committing.

keyPoints: Business policy is a whole-firm choice, not a sum of departmental answers.
Strategic fit requires internal consistency and external alignment.
Stakeholder trade-offs must respect legal, ethical and contractual limits.
Integrative case analysis moves from issue to options, criteria, decision and implementation.
Weighted score = Σ (weight × score); in the example B scores 3.7 against A’s 3.3.
Under uncertainty, use scenarios, pilots and stage gates, and review assumptions.
